title: Rootless Docker: Run Containers Without Root 🦾
description: Set up and use rootless mode so the Docker daemon and containers run as a normal user.

slides.title: The Risk of the Docker Daemon Running as Root 👑
slides.content:
# Why Rootless?

By default, the Docker daemon (`dockerd`) runs as root on the host. If an attacker escapes a container (rare but possible), they might gain root access to the host.

**Rootless mode** runs the entire Docker daemon and all containers as a non‑root user (using user namespaces and other tricks).

- The daemon runs inside a user namespace.
- Containers are further nested.
- Even if a container breakout occurs, the attacker gets only the unprivileged user’s permissions on the host.

> Available since Docker 19.03 (experimental) and production‑ready from 20.10+.

slides.title: How Rootless Works ⚙️
slides.content:
# User Namespaces + Slirp4netns

Rootless mode leverages:
- **User namespaces** to map the container’s root to an unprivileged UID on the host.
- **`rootlesskit`** to set up networking (using `slirp4netns` for tap device without root).
- **`fuse-overlayfs`** for storage driver (instead of overlay2 which needs root).

Limitations:
- Cannot bind to privileged ports (<1024) without adjusting `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_unprivileged_port_start`.
- Some features like `ping` need extra capabilities (`NET_RAW`), which may need to be added via sysctl.
- Slightly reduced networking performance (user‑mode networking).

quizData.question: What is the main security advantage of rootless Docker?

options.text: The daemon runs without root privileges, reducing host compromise risk
It uses a different container runtime

quizData.explanation: Rootless means even if an attacker breaks out of a container, they are not root on the host.

slides.title: Installing Rootless Docker 🛠️
slides.content:
# Step‑by‑Step Setup

On a Linux host with a normal user account:

1. Remove any existing rootful Docker (optional, they can coexist).
2. Install `uidmap` package:
   ```bash
   sudo apt install uidmap
   ```
3. Run the official install script:
   ```bash
   curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com/rootless | sh
   ```
   This installs Docker binaries in `~/.docker/` and sets up systemd user service.
4. Set environment variables (added to `~/.bashrc` by the script):
   ```bash
   export PATH=/home/$USER/bin:$PATH
   export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/user/1000/docker.sock
   ```
5. Start the daemon:
   ```bash
   systemctl --user start docker
   ```

Now `docker run hello-world` works as a non‑root user!

slides.title: Verify Rootless Operation 🔍
slides.content: Check that the daemon is not running as root:
slides.codeSnippet:
ps aux | grep dockerd
# Should show the daemon under your username, not root

docker info | grep -i rootless
# Should show: rootless: true

quizData.question: Rootless Docker can bind to privileged ports (below 1024) without any additional configuration.
quizData.explanation: By default, non‑root users cannot bind to ports <1024. You can lower `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` to allow it, but it's not enabled by default.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Rootless in Production
Rootless Docker is excellent for CI pipelines, development, and multi‑tenant environments. For production, evaluate the networking performance overhead and consider user namespace remapping (`userns-remap`) as an alternative if rootless is not feasible.
